title: Uber’s Zero Growth Stack: Scaling Services, While Optimising Infrastructure and AI Cost
gist: Uber's 'Zero Growth Stack' decouples infrastructure capacity from business growth via dynamic Go garbage-collection tuning (GOGCTunner reclaimed 70,000 CPU cores) and tighter AI coding-agent governance, after AI-related costs rose sixfold since 2024 and hit $2,000/developer/month, prompting a $1,500 usage cap and new AI-code-quality metrics.

insights.claim: Uber built a 'Zero Growth Stack' that decouples infrastructure capacity growth from business demand growth, letting the company shrink its physical hardware footprint while still scaling services.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: A template for large-scale operators to blunt data-center capex growth even as service demand rises — relevant to how hyperscale infra spend trends going forward.
insights.quote: Uber's "Zero Growth Stack" offers a scalable infrastructure solution that decouples capacity growth from business demand, allowing the company to reduce its physical hardware footprint while maintaining service scaling significantly.
insights.locator: Uber's "Zero Growth Stack" offers a scalable infrastructure

insights.claim: Static garbage-collection tuning failed at Uber because service memory footprints varied widely, from 100MB to 1GB, so uniform GOGC settings couldn't fit all workloads.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: Explains why hyperscale Go shops need workload-aware GC tuning rather than one-size-fits-all settings — a reusable diagnosis for any large polyglot fleet with heterogeneous memory profiles.
insights.quote: Recognising that static garbage collection (GC) tuning often failed to address services with highly varied memory footprints—ranging from 100MB to 1GB
insights.locator: A central pillar of this initiative is the systematic optimisation

insights.claim: Uber's GOGCTunner library dynamically adjusts the Go GOGC value by integrating with cgroup memory limits and monitoring live object utilisation, replacing static GC settings with a real-time control loop.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: A concrete, reusable pattern (cgroup-integrated, live-utilization-driven GC control) other engineering orgs running Go at scale could replicate to cut CPU/memory spend.
insights.locator: By integrating directly with cgroup memory limits

insights.claim: GOGCTunner's control loop keeps heap size at roughly 1.25x live objects while enforcing a strict 70% memory utilisation threshold to avoid out-of-memory events.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete tunable target (1.25x live-object heap, 70% utilisation ceiling) for teams designing similar dynamic GC governors.
insights.quote: heap size (maintained at 1.25x live objects) against strict 70% memory utilisation thresholds to avoid OOM events
insights.locator: While this automation successfully reclaimed 70,000 CPU cores

insights.claim: Uber's dynamic GC tuning via GOGCTunner reclaimed 70,000 CPU cores across 30 mission-critical services.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: A hard, quantified efficiency win from runtime-level optimisation — useful as a benchmark for the ROI of GC-tuning investments at scale.
insights.quote: this automation successfully reclaimed 70,000 CPU cores across 30 mission-critical services
insights.locator: While this automation successfully reclaimed 70,000 CPU cores

insights.claim: Uber structures its internal generative-AI development stack in four layers: a Platform Layer using Michelangelo AI as a model gateway, a Context Layer using an MCP Gateway to inject internal source code, a Specialised Layer deploying background agents like Minion and Shepherd, and a Review Layer using tools like uReview and Code Inbox.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: A reference architecture for how large enterprises are layering AI coding agents (gateway, context injection, specialised agents, review) — useful comparator for enterprise AI dev-tooling vendors and internal platform teams.
insights.locator: The architecture layers include a Platform Layer

insights.claim: 92% of Uber's engineers use AI coding agents monthly, and 31% of new code committed at Uber is now AI-authored.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: A concrete mid-2026 benchmark for AI-code-authorship penetration at a large-scale tech company, useful for calibrating how fast AI is displacing manual coding elsewhere.
insights.quote: 92% of engineers utilise these agents monthly—with 31% of new code being AI-authored
insights.locator: While 92% of engineers utilise these agents monthly

insights.claim: Uber's Autocover tool generates over 5,000 AI-written unit tests per month.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of AI-generated test output, which later becomes a cost/quality concern the company has to actively manage (see redundant-test overhead below).
insights.quote: Autocover generating over 5,000 unit tests per month
insights.locator: While 92% of engineers utilise these agents monthly

insights.claim: Uber's AI-related costs increased sixfold since 2024, driven by token-based billing models that led to budget exhaustion.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: A hard data point on real-world enterprise AI-opex growth trajectory — useful for modeling how fast AI coding-agent spend scales without controls.
insights.quote: AI-related costs increased sixfold since 2024, as token-based billing models led to budget exhaustion
insights.locator: the rapid adoption introduced significant economic friction

insights.claim: Individual Uber developer AI usage costs reached $2,000 per month by early 2026, prompting the company to cap per-developer AI spend at $1,500 monthly.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that unconstrained AI-agent usage costs can hit thousands of dollars per developer per month, making usage caps and FinOps-for-AI a near-term necessity for large engineering orgs.
insights.quote: individual developer costs reached $2,000 monthly by early 2026
insights.locator: the rapid adoption introduced significant economic friction

insights.claim: Uber shifted from unconstrained AI-tool adoption to strict cost governance, implementing hard usage caps limited to $1,500 per developer per month.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: Signals that consumption-based, token-billed AI coding tools carry real cost risk enterprises will actively rein in — a headwind for unchecked per-token pricing models and a tailwind for AI cost-governance tooling.
insights.quote: implementing usage caps limited to $1,500 per developer
insights.locator: To address these challenges, Uber transitioned from unconstrained adoption

themes.theme: New AI-code quality and efficiency metrics

insights.claim: Uber is auditing whether AI-generated code's productivity gains actually justify its infrastructure and quality overhead, moving away from assuming that more AI-generated code automatically equals more value.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: Signals a maturing, more skeptical phase of enterprise gen-AI-for-coding adoption after the initial hype cycle — watch for other large engineering orgs following suit with similar audits.
insights.locator: The company is now auditing the efficacy of AI-generated code

insights.claim: Uber proposes a 'net code quality ratio' that compares the frequency of post-release hotfixes between AI-authored and human-authored code, replacing reliance on aggregate revenue-per-labour and AI-compute-spend metrics.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: A candidate KPI for evaluating true ROI of AI coding tools beyond raw code-output volume — worth tracking as an emerging industry metric.
insights.quote: evaluating the "net code quality ratio", comparing the frequency of post-release hotfixes in AI-authored versus human-authored code
insights.locator: To evolve these metrics, teams are shifting

insights.claim: Uber is establishing a 'compute efficiency per feature' metric to weigh AI-generated code overhead — including redundant tests from tools like Autocover — against actual feature delivery and infrastructure sustainability goals.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: Points to a next-generation FinOps-for-AI metric that ties AI-agent compute cost directly to shipped feature value rather than raw activity — a pattern other engineering orgs may adopt.
